title: The Morning Brief: Regulators advance crypto infrastructure as Michigan escalates state-federal clash
dek: Friday brings four regulatory pivots: the CFTC moves to dismiss CME's challenge to crypto derivatives, the SEC formally embraces blockchain for securities recordkeeping, Michigan courts impose a $500K daily penalty on Kalshi in direct collision with CFTC authority, and Standard Chartered becomes the first Global Systemically Important Bank to offer spot Bitcoin and Ether trading in the UAE. Market sentiment reads at Greed (74), with bitcoin off 0.2% on the day but up 3.3% on the week.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The CFTC's attempt to dismiss CME's lawsuit and the SEC's blockchain transfer-agent proposal signal federal regulators moving toward crypto infrastructure codification, while Michigan's $500K daily penalty on Kalshi creates an immediate legal collision that will likely reach federal court and test whether state injunctions or federal emergency powers prevail.
bottom_line: Friday's regulatory moves signal federal authorities codifying crypto infrastructure into existing frameworks: the CFTC removing litigation barriers to derivatives approval, the SEC rewriting transfer-agent rules to accommodate blockchain recordkeeping, and Standard Chartered entering institutional trading in regulated jurisdictions. At the same time, Michigan's $500K daily penalty on Kalshi creates an unresolved collision between state court injunctions and federal emergency authority that will likely converge in federal court. The CFTC's dismissal motion outcome, the Michigan appeal and federal intervention, and the September 17 SEC roundtable on 24-hour trading are the near checkpoints that will test whether infrastructure clarity can survive state-level enforcement or whether federal authority supersedes it.
body: The picture on Friday is a regulatory push forward on multiple fronts, shadowed by a sharpening state-versus-federal conflict. The CFTC is fighting to clear the path for crypto derivatives at designated contract markets, the SEC is rewriting 40-year-old rules to accommodate tokenized securities, and a major bank is moving into institutional crypto trading outside the US, all on the same day a Michigan court has ordered a crypto exchange to block state residents or face daily penalties that contradict federal authorities' own emergency authorization to keep that exchange trading.

The CFTC's motion to dismiss CME's lawsuit stands as the day's most significant regulatory move toward infrastructure clarity. As the desk reported, the CFTC's lawyers characterized CME's challenge as lacking standing, arguing the exchange cannot show concrete financial injury from the CFTC's approval of Kalshi's Bitcoin perpetual contract. If the motion succeeds, it removes a litigation barrier that has blocked competitive derivatives offerings and signals that the CFTC's authority to approve crypto perpetual futures at DCMs will face fewer legal obstacles from incumbent exchanges. CME's next move, and whether the court grants the dismissal, will determine whether competitors can block rival crypto products through litigation or whether the CFTC's approval framework stands intact.

The SEC's proposed transfer-agent rulebook rewrite deepens this infrastructure momentum. For the first time since the early 1980s, the SEC is explicitly accommodating blockchain-native recordkeeping, distributed ledger platforms, and tokenized securities within the regulatory framework that governs who maintains the official record of securities ownership. Per the reporting, the SEC's 421-page proposal opens space for blockchain-based transfer agents, tokenization platforms, and smart-contract-driven issuance processes. The same day, the SEC announced a September 17 roundtable on 24-hour US stock trading, suggesting the infrastructure modernization extends to market structure itself. Both moves, derivatives approval pathways and tokenization-ready transfer-agent rules, mark a shift from regulatory hostility toward crypto-adjacent infrastructure to codifying it into existing market frameworks.

Michigan's preliminary injunction on Kalshi, however, creates a direct and immediate collision. As the desk reported, Ingham County Circuit Judge Rosemarie Aquilina issued an order on September 2 requiring Kalshi to geofence Michigan residents and bar them from sports prediction wagering, with a $500,000-per-day penalty for non-compliance. The order stands until final judgment and arrives as the CFTC has already invoked emergency powers to keep Kalshi trading nationally. Kalshi now faces a binary choice: comply with Michigan's state injunction and lose the state entirely, or comply with the CFTC's federal authorization and accrue $500K daily penalties. This collision will likely reach federal court and turn on whether federal emergency authority overrides state injunctions or whether state court findings of irreparable harm hold.

Outside the US, Standard Chartered moved onto institutional spot Bitcoin and Ether trading in the UAE on September 3, becoming the first Global Systemically Important Bank to offer the service in the country. The move follows the bank's 2024 UAE custody launch and 2025 London crypto trading desk. It signals that major institutional finance is willing to embed crypto infrastructure in regulated non-US jurisdictions when the regulatory framework is clear, a pattern that parallels the SEC and CFTC's own domestic moves toward clarity.

On the protocol side, Core DAO announced an emergency hard fork after a validator reward bug allowed validators to draw excess rewards. Coinbase and four other exchanges restricted CORE transfers. Core stated the planned forward upgrade will not roll back the network or reverse previously confirmed transactions, marking a commitment to move forward without reversing confirmed state, a distinction that matters as the network attempts to contain validator-level protocol flaws.
